text: Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: You have seen everything the LORD did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh, to all his servants, and to all his land—
the great trials your eyes witnessed, those great signs and wonders.
Yet to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear.
I led you forty years in the wilderness. Your clothes did not wear out on you, and the sandals on your feet did not wear out.
You ate no bread and drank no wine or strong drink, so that you would know that I am the LORD your God.
When you came to this place, Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan marched out to meet us in battle, and we defeated them.
We took their land and gave it as an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
So keep the words of this covenant and carry them out, that you may prosper in everything you do.
Today all of you are standing before the LORD your God—your tribal leaders, your elders and your officers, every man of Israel,
your children and your wives, and the foreigner in your camp, from the one who chops your wood to the one who draws your water—
to enter into the covenant of the LORD your God and into his sworn oath, which the LORD your God is making with you today,
so that he may establish you today as his people and be your God, as he promised you and as he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
It is not with you alone that I am making this covenant with its oath,
but with everyone standing here with us today before the LORD our God, and also with those who are not here with us today.
For you know how we lived in the land of Egypt, and how we passed through the nations you traveled among.

versions.text: You know how we lived in the land of Egypt, and how we passed through the midst of the nations along the way.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew ends with a second verb, "the nations through which you passed," which the vague phrase "along the way" drops. Restoring the relative clause keeps the content while staying readable.

versions.text: You know how we lived in the land of Egypt, and how we passed through the nations you traveled among.
versions.explanation: The opening כִּי links this verse explanatorily to the preceding covenant statement. Dropping it leaves the sentence floating; restoring "For" preserves the logical connective and helps the flow when read aloud.

text: You saw their detestable things and their idols of wood and stone, of silver and gold, that they kept among them.

Make sure there is no man or woman, no clan or tribe among you whose heart turns away today from the LORD our God to go and serve the gods of those nations—make sure there is no root among you bearing poison and bitterness.

When such a person hears the words of this oath, he congratulates himself in his heart and says, "I will be safe, even though I walk in the stubbornness of my own heart." This would sweep away the watered land along with the dry.

The LORD will never be willing to forgive him. Instead, the LORD's anger and jealousy will smolder against that man, every curse written in this book will settle on him, and the LORD will blot out his name from under heaven.
The LORD will single him out from all the tribes of Israel for disaster, in keeping with all the curses of the covenant written in this Book of the Law.
The next generation, your children who come after you, and the foreigner who arrives from a distant land, will see the plagues of that land and the diseases the LORD has inflicted on it—

the whole land a burning waste of sulfur and salt, unsown, yielding nothing, with not a blade of grass growing on it, like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and wrath.

versions.text: the whole land a burning waste of sulfur and salt, unsown, yielding nothing, with not a blade of grass growing on it, like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his fierce anger.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two nouns, "his anger and his wrath"; "his fierce anger" collapses the pair and loses the intensity of the doubled expression.

text: All the nations will ask, "Why has the LORD done this to this land? Why this great outburst of anger?"
And the answer will be: "Because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers, the covenant he made with them when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.
They went and served other gods and bowed down to them, gods they had not known, gods he had not assigned to them.
So the LORD's anger burned against that land, bringing upon it every curse written in this book.

versions.text: So the LORD's anger burned against this land, and he brought upon it every curse written in this book.
versions.explanation: Hebrew הַהִוא means "that land," matching the distant reference in verse 21; "this land" wrongly shifts the perspective to the speaker's present location.

versions.text: So the LORD's anger burned against that land, and he brought upon it every curse written in this book.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew uses an infinitive of purpose/result (לְהָבִיא), not a second finite verb. A participial phrase keeps the subordinate, result-oriented sense while reading smoothly; "and he brought" turns it into an independent action.

text: The LORD uprooted them from their soil in anger and wrath and great fury, and cast them into another land, as it is today."
The hidden things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may carry out all the words of this law.
